chunks: Abu Ali Al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Sa'id ibn Yasar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), regarding

A man handed over wealth to another man and said, 'I am only handing it to you to be a reserve for my two daughters, So-and-so and So-and-so.' Then the old man changed his mind after handing over the wealth and took from it one hundred and twenty-five dinars, and bought a slave girl for his grandson. Then the old man died. A dispute arose between the two girls and the boy (or one of them), and they said to him, 'Woe to you, by Allah, you are marrying your slave girl unlawfully. Our father bought her for you from our wealth which he handed over to So-and-so, so he bought this slave girl for you from it. So you are marrying her unlawfully; she is not permissible for you.' So the youth refrained from the slave girl. What do you think about that? He (peace be upon him) said, 'Is not the man who handed over the wealth the father of the two girls, and he is the grandfather of the boy, and he is the one who bought the slave girl for him?' I said, 'Yes.' He said, 'So tell him, let him go to his slave girl, since it was the grandfather who gave it to him and he is the one who took it.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on marriage to a slave girl purchased with funds entrusted by her father to the grandfather?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Kafi* illustrates the Shia juristic principle of *istihsan* (juristic preference) or contextual interpretation, where the Imam prioritizes the substantive role of the fund provider (the grandfather) over the technical ownership of the specific funds to permit marriage. It highlights the flexibility in *fiqh al-muwala* (kinship-based transactions), distinguishing between the source of wealth and the resulting legal status of the acquired property, thereby resolving the daughters' claim of impediment (*'illat*) based on their contribution.
